items.stem: Why was the Berlin Wall built in 1961? Give one reason.
items.answer: About 2.7 million East Germans had left for the West, many through Berlin.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid reason, for example: About 2.7 million East Germans had left for the West, many through Berlin. Many of those leaving were young, skilled workers such as doctors and engineers. The loss of workers damaged the East German economy. West Berlin's prosperity was an embarrassment to communism. Khrushchev had failed to force the West out of Berlin at the Vienna summit. [1]

options: It argues the USSR signed the pact defensively because the West had refused to cooperate.
It suggests Hitler was planning expansion by force in a clear sequence.
Chamberlain suggests that Britain should not go to war over Czechoslovakia, a distant dispute that did not concern Britain directly.

items.stem: Why were relations between Britain and Germany tense before 1914? Give two reasons.
items.answer: The naval race threatened Britain's naval supremacy, on which its empire and trade depended. Kaiser Wilhelm II's “world policy” (Weltpolitik) sought colonies and influence that challenged Britain.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each valid reason, any two from: The naval race threatened Britain's naval supremacy, on which its empire and trade depended. Kaiser Wilhelm II's “world policy” (Weltpolitik) sought colonies and influence that challenged Britain. German actions in the Moroccan crises of 1905 and 1911 pushed Britain closer to France. Economic rivalry grew as German industry overtook Britain's in steel production. [2]

items.stem: How far was containment a success in Asia between 1950 and 1975? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: South Korea was saved from communism. Taiwan, Japan, Thailand and the Philippines remained non-communist. SEATO and US bases restricted communist expansion. Against: China became communist in 1949. Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia all became communist in 1975. The Vietnam War damaged US prestige and cost huge sums and lives. Judgement: Containment had mixed results: it succeeded in Korea and much of the region, but its failure in Vietnam was a major defeat.

Possible judgement: Containment had mixed results: it succeeded in Korea and much of the region, but its failure in Vietnam was a major defeat. [10]

items.stem: How far did the Big Three agree about how Germany should be treated? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: All agreed Germany should be punished in some way, disarmed and lose some territory. All agreed Alsace-Lorraine should go back to France and that Belgium should be restored. Against: Clemenceau wanted Germany crippled; Wilson wanted a just peace. Lloyd George wanted Germany to recover as a trading partner. They clashed over the Rhineland, the Saar, reparations and freedom of the seas. items.stem: Source C is Point 10 of President Wilson's Fourteen Points, January 1918. “The peoples of Austria-Hungary, whose place among the nations we wish to see safeguarded and assured, should be accorded the freest opportunity to autonomous development.” Study the source. (a) What impression does Source C give of Wilson's idea of self-determination? Explain your answer using details of the source. [6] (b) Use your own knowledge to explain one thing about Wilson's plans for the peace that Source C does not tell us. [3]
items.answer: (a) Wilson wanted the nationalities of Austria-Hungary to be allowed to govern themselves. Purpose / point of view of the author: to support the national groups of Austria-Hungary and weaken the enemy alliance. (b) That Austria-Hungary would collapse completely by November 1918 and new states would be created.

items.stem: Read Source D carefully. “How horrible, fantastic, incredible it is that we should be digging trenches and trying on gas-masks here because of a quarrel in a far away country between people of whom we know nothing.” (A radio broadcast by Neville Chamberlain to the British people, 27 September 1938 (extract).) (a) What impression does Source D give of Chamberlain's attitude to the Sudeten crisis? Explain your answer using details of the source. [6] (b) Use your own knowledge to explain one thing about the policy of appeasement that Source D does not tell us. [3]
items.answer: (a) Chamberlain suggests that Britain should not go to war over Czechoslovakia, a distant dispute that did not concern Britain directly. Purpose / point of view of the author: to prepare the British people for a peaceful settlement and justify his efforts to avoid war. (b) That Britain's military chiefs had warned the country was not ready for war.

items.stem: Study Source C. Source C: an article in a Japanese newspaper, 1931 (illustrative). “Our farmers are ruined since America stopped buying our silk. Manchuria, with its coal, iron and land, is Japan's lifeline. The government must act.” (a) What impression does Source C give of Japanese attitudes during the Depression? Explain your answer using details of the source. [6] (b) Does Source C support the view that the Depression was the main reason the League failed in the 1930s? items.stem: Why did Germany ask for an armistice in 1918? Give one reason.
items.answer: The Ludendorff (Spring) Offensive failed and exhausted the German army.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid reason, for example: The Ludendorff (Spring) Offensive failed and exhausted the German army. The Allied Hundred Days Offensive from August 1918 pushed the Germans back. Fresh American troops were arriving in large numbers. The British blockade caused hunger and unrest at home, ending in mutiny and revolution. Germany's allies Bulgaria, the Ottoman Empire and Austria-Hungary all made peace in autumn 1918. [1]

items.stem: Study Source C. Source C: an extract from a modern history textbook (illustrative). “The League was not a world government. It could only be as strong as its members wanted it to be, and in the 1930s its most powerful members wanted to avoid war at almost any price.” Which statement best describes the message of Source C?
options: It argues the League's weakness was the reluctance of its members, not just its structure.
It argues the League's slow procedures, rather than the bad faith of its members, explain the failure in Manchuria.
It shows small countries valued the equality the Assembly gave them.
It shows world trade fell by about two-thirds between January 1929 and January 1933.
items.answer: It argues the League's weakness was the reluctance of its members, not just its structure.
items.markingKey: Only this statement matches the content of Source C. [1]

items.stem: A revision website states: “The Marshall Plan was mainly military aid.” Is this accurate? Explain your answer using your own knowledge.
items.answer: Not accurate. It was economic aid for recovery: food, machinery, fuel and loans.

items.stem: Study Source A. Source A: a report by an American war correspondent, 1967 (illustrative). “We can hold any ground we choose, but the moment we leave a village the Viet Cong return. Every burnt hut makes a new recruit for them.” What can you infer from Source A about US tactics in Vietnam? Support your answer with a detail from the source.
items.answer: It suggests US tactics could not achieve lasting control and turned villagers against the USA. Supporting detail: for example, “We can hold any ground we choose, but the moment we leave a village the Viet Cong return”.

items.stem: Why was Hitler able to rearm Germany without being stopped? Give two reasons.
items.answer: Many in Britain felt Germany had been unfairly disarmed by Versailles. Germany's neighbours had not disarmed, so Hitler claimed he only wanted equality.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each valid reason, any two from: Many in Britain felt Germany had been unfairly disarmed by Versailles. Germany's neighbours had not disarmed, so Hitler claimed he only wanted equality. The League's disarmament conference had failed. Britain made the Anglo-German Naval Agreement, accepting German rearmament. Britain and France were preoccupied with the Depression. [1]

items.stem: Germany lost about 13 per cent of its European territory under the Treaty of Versailles. Describe the territorial terms of the Treaty of Versailles.
items.answer: Alsace-Lorraine was returned to France. West Prussia and Posen went to Poland, creating the Polish Corridor. Danzig became a Free City under the League. The Saar was run by the League for 15 years. Eupen and Malmedy went to Belgium and North Schleswig to Denmark after a plebiscite. Germany's colonies became League mandates.
items.markingKey: One mark for each relevant point; a further mark for supporting detail, up to 4 marks. Indicative content: Alsace-Lorraine was returned to France. West Prussia and Posen went to Poland, creating the Polish Corridor. Danzig became a Free City under the League. The Saar was run by the League for 15 years. Eupen and Malmedy went to Belgium and North Schleswig to Denmark after a plebiscite. Germany's colonies became League mandates. [4]

items.stem: Paper 1 (a)-style question. Describe the naval race between Britain and Germany before 1914.
items.answer: Germany's Navy Laws from 1898 began a large expansion of its fleet. Britain launched HMS Dreadnought in 1906, a faster, more heavily armed battleship. Germany began building its own dreadnoughts, so both raced to build more. British public pressure led to the slogan “We want eight and we won't wait” in 1909. Britain kept the lead, with more dreadnoughts than Germany by 1914.

items.stem: Read Source A carefully. “Mr Wilson speaks of justice, but he has not seen the ruined towns of our northern departments. France needs guarantees, not fine words, and Germany must pay for what it has destroyed.” (An editorial in a French newspaper, early 1919 (illustrative).) What does Source A tell you about French attitudes to Wilson's ideas? Use details of the source to support your answer.
items.answer: French opinion felt Wilson's ideas were too soft on Germany and that France needed security and compensation. Supporting details: for example, “Mr Wilson speaks of justice, but he has not seen the ruined towns of our northern departments”; each detail should be linked to an inference.

items.stem: Why did the USA not join the League of Nations? Give two reasons.
items.answer: The Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles, which included the League Covenant. Many Americans wanted isolationism after heavy losses in a European war.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each valid reason, any two from: The Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles, which included the League Covenant. Many Americans wanted isolationism after heavy losses in a European war. They feared Article 10 might force the USA to send troops to defend other countries. Some thought membership would harm American trade, for example through sanctions. Party politics: Republicans opposed the Democrat Wilson. [2]

items.stem: Source A is Stalin's response to Churchill's Fulton speech, published in the Soviet newspaper Pravda, March 1946 (summary). Stalin said that the USSR had lost far more people than Britain and the USA together in the war, and that it was natural for it to want governments friendly to the USSR in the countries through which Germany had attacked. He compared Churchill to Hitler as a warmonger. Study the source. (a) How useful is Source A as evidence about the Soviet takeover of eastern Europe? Explain your answer using details of the source and your knowledge. [7] (b) Use your own knowledge to explain one thing about the Soviet takeover of eastern Europe that Source A does not tell us. [3]
items.answer: (a) Useful: Stalin argues that Soviet control of eastern Europe was a natural defensive response to the war. Provenance: it gives Stalin's own justification. Limitations: it is propaganda in a state-controlled newspaper and ignores how communists were seizing power. It does not show: The use of salami tactics and rigged elections, as in Poland in 1947. (b) The use of salami tactics and rigged elections, as in Poland in 1947.

items.stem: Source B is a statement by President Truman, 27 June 1950 (summary). Truman announced that he had ordered US air and sea forces to support South Korea, saying that the attack showed communism had moved beyond subversion to the use of armed invasion and war. Study the source. (a) How useful is Source B as evidence about the Korean War? Explain your answer using details of the source and your knowledge. items.answer: (a) Useful: Truman presents the invasion as communist aggression that had to be resisted. Provenance: it is the President's own explanation at the time. items.stem: Read Source E carefully. “Versailles was not the cause of the war in 1939, but it provided Hitler with the excuses and the popular support he needed. Without the treaty, his message would have found far fewer listeners.” (An extract from a modern history textbook (illustrative).) (a) Does Source E support the view that the Treaty of Versailles was the main long-term cause of the Second World War? Explain your answer using details of the source and your knowledge. [6] (b) How reliable is Source E as an account of the role of the Treaty of Versailles? Explain your answer. [6]
items.answer: (a) Supports: it gives the treaty a central role in Hitler's rise and policies However, it is a short extract and does not discuss other factors in detail. (b) Reliable because it is written with hindsight and reaches a balanced view. Less reliable because it is a short extract and does not discuss other factors in detail. Judgement: reliable as evidence of this point of view on the role of the Treaty of Versailles, but it needs cross-checking with other evidence.

items.stem: How important was Solidarity in the collapse of communism in eastern Europe? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: It was the first independent mass movement in the Soviet bloc. It survived martial law and won the 1989 elections, showing others the way. Against: Without Gorbachev's refusal to intervene, Solidarity might have been crushed again. Economic decline undermined all the communist regimes. Events in Hungary and East Germany had their own causes. Judgement: Solidarity was very important as an example, but it succeeded in 1989 because Gorbachev would not intervene.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1): general answer. Level 2 (2-3): identifies and/or describes. Level 3 (4-6): explains one side. Level 4 (7-9): explains both sides. Level 5 (10): explains both sides and reaches a supported judgement on "how far" / "how important". Agree / supporting: It was the first independent mass movement in the Soviet bloc. It survived martial law and won the 1989 elections, showing others the way. Disagree / other factors: Without Gorbachev's refusal to intervene, Solidarity might have been crushed again. Economic decline undermined all the communist regimes. Events in Hungary and East Germany had their own causes. Possible judgement: Solidarity was very important as an example, but it succeeded in 1989 because Gorbachev would not intervene. [10]

items.stem: Source B is a cartoon by Leonard Raven-Hill published in the British magazine Punch, 10 December 1919, titled “The Gap in the Bridge”. A bridge labelled with the names of the Allied countries forms the “League of Nations”, but the keystone in the middle is missing. Uncle Sam, representing the USA, leans against the missing stone, smoking a pipe. The caption says the bridge was designed by the President of the USA. Study the source. Why was Source B published at this time? Explain your answer using details of the source and your knowledge.
items.answer: To comment on the US Senate's vote against the treaty in November 1919 and its consequences for the League. Context: The US Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles on 19 November 1919.

items.stem: Consider the question “Why were several new states created in Europe in 1918-19?” Here are some reasons: P: Nationalist movements among Poles, Czechs, Slovaks and South Slavs declared independence. Q: The Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires collapsed, leaving their peoples without a government. R: Wilson's principle of self-determination encouraged the Allies to recognise national states. Explain how each reason contributed, show how at least two of them were linked, and decide which was the most important. Justify your choice.
items.answer: Explains each reason in turn; links, for example, how one reason made another more serious; reaches a judgement on the most important reason with criteria (e.g. which made the outcome certain, or which came first and caused the others).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): describes reasons. Level 2 (3-5): explains reasons separately. Level 3 (6-8): explains and links reasons. Level 4 (9-10): explains and links reasons and reaches a supported judgement on relative importance [10]

items.stem: Study Source B, a photograph taken in West Berlin in 1948 (description). A crowd of Berliners stands on a pile of rubble near Tempelhof airport, watching an American transport plane flying low overhead as it comes in to land. (a) What impression does Source B give of the Berlin Airlift? Explain your answer using details of the source. [6] (b) Does Source B support the view that the Berlin Blockade was a victory for the West? Explain your answer using details of the source and your knowledge. [6]
items.answer: (a) It suggests Berliners welcomed the airlift and depended on it. Purpose / point of view of the author: to record and publicise the success of the airlift. (b) Supports: it shows the airlift succeeding with Berliners' support However, photographs like this were widely used as Western propaganda, and it shows only one moment.
